questions.q: What is the key difference between slippage and spread cost?
options: They are the same thing with different names

Spread cost is the implicit cost of crossing the bid-ask spread; slippage is the difference between the expected trade price and the actual fill price, which can be caused by market movement or the order's own impact
Slippage only applies to bonds, spread cost only applies to stocks
Spread cost is always larger than slippage
questions.explain: Spread cost specifically refers to crossing the bid-ask spread; slippage is a broader concept covering any gap between the expected and actual execution price, including from market movement between decision and fill.

questions.q: In the cost model `cost = position.diff().abs() * price * (cost_bps / 10000)`, why is the cost based on `position.diff()` rather than the position itself?
options: Because position.diff() is easier to compute
Because trading costs are incurred when a position CHANGES (a trade occurs), not simply for holding an existing position
Because position.diff() always equals zero
Because costs should be charged every day regardless of trading
questions.explain: Transaction costs are incurred by the act of trading. Holding a static position overnight doesn't trigger a trade, so cost should only be charged on the change in position, which represents an actual buy or sell.

questions.q: Why should a realistic slippage model scale with recent volatility rather than use a fixed constant?
options: Volatility has no real relationship to execution quality
Slippage tends to be worse in volatile or illiquid conditions and smaller in calm, liquid markets, so a fixed assumption misrepresents both regimes
Fixed slippage models are always more accurate than volatility-based ones
Volatility only matters for options trading
questions.explain: Markets that are choppier or less liquid make it harder to execute near the last quoted price, so slippage realistically increases with volatility rather than staying constant.

questions.q: In a correctly modeled backtest, should slippage ever work IN FAVOR of the trader (i.e. fill better than the quoted price) on average?
options: Yes, roughly half the time, since it's random noise
No — slippage should be modeled as consistently working against the trader on average, since that reflects real competitive execution
Yes, always, since markets are efficient
It doesn't matter which direction slippage is modeled
questions.explain: Real-world execution costs work against the trader on average — buys fill slightly higher, sells slightly lower. A model where slippage randomly helps the trader is not modeling real market friction.

questions.q: Why does a high-turnover strategy suffer disproportionately from transaction costs compared to a low-turnover strategy with the same underlying signal?
options: High-turnover strategies always have weaker signals
Because transaction costs are charged on each position change, so a strategy that trades daily pays the round-trip cost far more often per year than one that trades monthly
Transaction costs are fixed per year regardless of trade frequency
High-turnover strategies are exempt from commissions
questions.explain: Since cost is proportional to trading frequency, a daily-rebalancing strategy can pay its round-trip cost roughly 252 times a year versus about 12 times for a monthly strategy — a large enough difference to flip a strategy from profitable to unprofitable.
